$comment: Every word and every editorial choice on the profile lives here. README.md and profile/pages/*.md are generated from this file plus the GitHub API — never edit them by hand. Run: node scripts/generate-profile.mjs

nav.$comment: The one centred row under the banner: where you can go inside this profile. `to` is a page id from `groups`. There is no second row of outward links — LinkedIn, ORCID and npm are in the footer, which is where somebody looks when they have finished reading rather than before they have started.

$opening: One line, centred, above everything else — before the banner, before any link. It is the first thing on the page, so it should sound like a person rather than a summary. The previous one, kept here in case it is wanted back: "A service that answers every request and gets none of them right is still down. It just hasn't noticed yet."
opening: I learned most of this by getting it wrong first.

banner.$comment: The strip at the top. No name and no job title on purpose: GitHub already prints both in the sidebar right next to it, so putting them in the one image everybody sees first would spend it on a repeat. It shows the ground I actually cover instead — one chip per facet, in whatever order reads best. Add or remove a facet and the banner redraws around it. `glyph` has to be one of the drawings in GLYPHS inside the generator.

quickAccess.$comment: The launcher rows under the nav. Fifteen slots at most: up to `maxPinned` chosen here by hand, and `recentCount` filled automatically with whatever was pushed to most recently — that half is the only part of this profile that reorders itself. Rows are unlabelled and unruled on purpose; ranging them right against the centred navigation above is enough to tell the two apart. A private entry needs `private: true` and its own `label`, since the token this runs under cannot read the repository to find one.
quickAccess.$rows: There is no `orgs` row: a row of somebody else's repositories under my own read as their work on my page. An automatic entry whose row is not listed here is simply dropped, so today the five automatic slots only fill when one of my own repositories is the most recently pushed — and everything of mine worth a shortcut is pinned below.
quickAccess.$exclude: didactika/.github is the organisation's own profile page and regenerates itself on a schedule, so it would win 'most recently pushed' every single day without anybody having worked on it.

about.$comment: A list rather than paragraphs, so it can be read at the speed people actually read a profile. One idea per line, no line running past two.
about.heading: About
points: Computer engineer, five years building software. Degree at Universidad Europea del Atlántico, master's in cybersecurity at UNIR.
Backend and event-driven systems: queues, retries, and the integrations that hold a university's systems together.
I would rather learn a job by doing it than by reading about it, and I go looking for the problems that did not work the first time.
At my best where an idea can be tried instead of argued about.
Happy to lead a project when it needs someone to, and happier still with people around to do it with.
There is a life outside this. When the two collide I finish what I owe first.

groups.label: Packages
groups.blurb: TypeScript libraries for Node.js backends — messaging, HTTP and data access.
groups.page: Libraries I publish and maintain on npm. Each one came out of a real service that needed it twice.

groups.label: Moodle
groups.blurb: Plugins and clients that extend Moodle for integration-heavy campuses.
groups.page: Moodle work — local plugins, themes and the web-service client that ties external systems into a campus.

projects.name: @resilientmq/core
projects.desc: Resilient event processing for RabbitMQ. Declares which events a consumer handles, then takes care of everything that can go wrong around them: retry policy, dead-letter routing, per-event state so a redelivery is not reprocessed, and a controlled way to mark an event as deliberately ignored rather than failed.

projects.name: @didactika/prisma-autoread
projects.desc: Drop-in search endpoints for Express and Prisma. One declaration yields filtering, sorting, field selection, relation includes, aggregations and both offset and cursor pagination — over GET, the new QUERY method or POST — emitting HAL, JSON:API or CSV.

projects.name: http-response-client
projects.desc: One shape for every response an Express service returns, success or failure. Typed constructors for the standard HTTP errors, custom errors on the same contract, and middleware that turns a thrown error into a well-formed body instead of a stack trace.

projects.name: moodle-web-service-client
projects.desc: Typed Node.js client for the Moodle web-service API. Handles Moodle's flattened parameter encoding and its habit of returning errors with a 200, so callers get a rejected promise instead of a body they have to inspect.

projects.name: @resilientmq/mongoose-connector
projects.desc: MongoDB storage backend for ResilientMQ. Persists event state through Mongoose so consumer restarts and redeliveries stay idempotent.

projects.name: moodle-local_digitalta
projects.desc: Local plugin behind DigitalTA on Moodle 4.1 — the data model, pages and services for the platform's teaching-assistant workflow.

projects.name: moodle-theme_digitalta
projects.desc: Companion theme for DigitalTA: layouts, SCSS and Mustache templates that give the plugin its own interface rather than a skinned Boost.

tracked.$comment: Public repositories that feed the charts. `owned` is discovered from the API; list here the ones I contribute to but do not own. Private repositories are deliberately absent — the Actions token cannot read them, and a chart that silently drops half the data is worse than a smaller honest one.
